correction: MIDI regions can contain notes plus control change, pitch bend, aftertouch, and other events; the event type, channel, time, and value determine what the instrument receives.
myth: midi controller events beyond notes has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the MIDI region, open an event view that exposes non-note data, filter to one controller type, and compare playback before changing anything.

correction: Sustain is controller data, commonly CC64, and a missing or late pedal-up event can keep notes ringing even when note events have ended.
myth: sustain pedal / cc64 and stuck ringing has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: On a duplicate region, locate the sustain events around the stuck passage and move or insert only the pedal-up event, then compare the same phrase.

correction: Sustain data may be easier to inspect in a controller lane or the Event List than in the note display, and it belongs to the MIDI region rather than the instrument plug-in itself.
myth: finding and editing sustain-pedal data has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region, display only CC64 events, and identify the nearest pedal-down and pedal-up pair before moving either event.

correction: Pedal timing controls how harmonies overlap; moving pedal-up slightly before or after a chord change can trade continuity for clarity.
myth: pedal timing, harmony changes, and overlap has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Copy the region and move one pedal-up event around a problematic chord change by a small amount while listening in context.

correction: Some instruments and pedals interpret intermediate sustain values, while others behave mainly as on/off switches; the instrument implementation must be checked before assuming half-pedal behavior.
myth: half-pedaling and continuous sustain values has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Record or draw a short pedal ramp on a duplicate region and compare whether the instrument responds continuously or switches at a threshold.

correction: Mod-wheel movement is usually recorded as MIDI controller data and may control vibrato, timbre, dynamics, or a custom destination depending on the instrument.
myth: modulation-wheel / cc1 data has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region, isolate CC1 events, flatten or redraw only the questionable passage, and compare while watching the instrument response.

correction: CC11 commonly scales expression within the broader level established by CC7, but instrument mappings vary; neither is automatically the same as Logic track volume automation.
myth: expression cc11 versus channel volume cc7 has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: On a duplicate region, inspect CC7 and CC11 separately and temporarily bypass one stream to identify which one causes the level change.

correction: Pitch bend is a dedicated high-resolution MIDI message whose audible range is set by the receiving instrument, so the same curve can produce different intervals on different patches.
myth: pitch bend events and bend range has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region, inspect the bend events and the instrument bend range, then center or redraw one problematic bend while preserving the original.

correction: Channel pressure, polyphonic pressure, foot controllers, breath data, and other CC messages may be recorded even when the user only intended to capture notes.
myth: aftertouch and other midi controllers has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Filter a duplicate region by event type and mute one suspected stream at a time to identify which controller changes the sound.

correction: Accidental controller data should be identified by event type, channel, and time range before deletion; deleting all non-note events can remove legitimate performance information.
myth: deleting accidental controller data has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region, select only the suspected controller type in the affected range, delete it, and compare against the original.

correction: MIDI CC data lives inside MIDI regions and is sent to the instrument, while track automation controls Logic channel-strip or plug-in parameters on the timeline; the owner determines whether copying a region carries the movement.
myth: midi controller data versus track automation has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Create a duplicate region and a temporary track-automation lane for the same audible parameter, then compare which follows region copies and which remains timeline-based.

correction: Moving notes does not always move every non-note event unless Logic is told to include related MIDI data; controller curves can become detached from the notes they were meant to shape.
myth: moving notes with related controller data has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region, move one phrase with related non-note MIDI included, and compare it with a note-only move.

correction: Precise MIDI editing depends on seeing the correct region, time range, pitch range, and grid resolution before moving notes.
myth: piano roll navigation and zoom has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Open the target MIDI region, zoom until note starts and ends are clear, and verify the playhead and selected-region scope before editing.

correction: Smart Snap changes its effective grid with zoom and ruler division, which is convenient for broad edits but can feel unpredictable during precise work.
myth: smart snap in the piano roll has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the MIDI region, note the current Snap mode, zoom in, and move one test note while watching the help tag.

correction: Relative Snap preserves a note’s offset from the grid when moved, while absolute snapping places it directly on the chosen grid position.
myth: relative versus absolute snap has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: On a duplicate region, move one deliberately off-grid note once with relative snap and once with absolute snap, then compare both timing results.

correction: Control-modified dragging can temporarily increase edit precision without changing the project’s normal Snap setting.
myth: temporary snap override and tick-level editing has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region, start dragging one note, use the temporary fine-grid modifier, and confirm the position in the help tag or Event Float.

correction: Dragging is fast, while nudge commands and numerical entry provide repeatable increments; the best method depends on whether the edit is visual, musical, or exact.
myth: dragging, nudging, and fine note adjustment has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Select a duplicate phrase, set a known nudge value, move it one step earlier, and compare against the original at the same tempo.

correction: Group moves should preserve internal note relationships unless the user intentionally wants to revoice or spread the chord.
myth: moving chords and groups of notes has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Select the complete chord or phrase in a duplicated region, constrain horizontal movement, and nudge it once while checking that all note starts moved equally.

correction: Multiple selected notes can be resized proportionally or made the same length; those are different operations and can change legato, gaps, and articulation.
myth: batch editing midi note lengths has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region, select the target notes, choose proportional or equal-length behavior deliberately, and audition with the instrument release unchanged.

correction: Overlapping notes can create legato, retrigger, voice-stealing, or stuck-note behavior depending on the instrument; visible overlap is not automatically wrong.
myth: overlapping notes, legato, and gaps has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: On a duplicate region, trim one problematic overlap to a small gap and compare it against the original.

correction: Selection scope determines whether a batch edit affects one chord, one pitch class, a velocity range, or the complete region.
myth: selecting and editing groups of midi notes has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region, use a visual or conditional selection for one clearly defined group, then apply one small edit and verify what remained untouched.

correction: The Event Float and Event List expose exact bar/beat/tick positions and values when mouse movement is not precise enough.
myth: event float and numerical midi positioning has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region, select one note, record its current position, enter one exact small offset, and compare.

correction: Time Handles scale the timing of selected notes around a pivot; they are useful for compressing or expanding a phrase, not for repairing one isolated note.
myth: time handles and proportional midi scaling has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region, select one phrase, set the handles around it, and make a very small proportional timing change.

correction: The Piano Roll can display data from more than one MIDI region, so color, selection, and link state matter when editing layered parts.
myth: multiple regions in the piano roll has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the project state, select only the intended region, and verify note color/selection before making one edit.

correction: A project bounce renders the selected output over the chosen start/end or cycle range; an incorrect range can omit pickups, count-ins, or tails.
myth: project bounce range and cycle scope has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Create a Project Alternative, set a short test bounce range that includes the musical start and extra tail time, then compare the file against playback.

correction: Offline bounce can render internal sources faster than playback, while external MIDI, live inputs, or hardware-dependent paths may require realtime.
myth: realtime versus offline bounce has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Bounce the same short internal-only section offline and realtime, then null or compare the files before choosing a mode for the final export.

correction: A bounce range based only on the last region can end before instrument releases, reverb, or delay have decayed.
myth: including reverb, delay, and instrument tails has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Make a short test bounce with extra end time or Include Audio Tail and compare the final seconds on headphones.

correction: Normalization changes file level after rendering; Off, overload-only, and full normalization serve different purposes and do not replace mix or mastering decisions.
myth: bounce and export normalization has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Bounce a short section with normalization Off and compare it to an overload-protection test at matched playback level.

correction: PCM formats preserve uncompressed sample data, while MP3/AAC and other lossy formats trade data for smaller files; destination determines the appropriate choice.
myth: pcm versus compressed export formats has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Export one short reference as PCM and one as the intended compressed format, level-match, and audition critical transients and high-frequency material.

correction: Sample rate, bit depth, and dither are delivery choices with different consequences; dither is relevant when reducing word length, not as a general tone enhancer.
myth: sample rate, bit depth, and dither has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Create a short 24-bit PCM reference and the required lower-bit-depth deliverable using one deliberate dither stage, then compare at a realistic level.

correction: Track in Place renders a track and its chosen processing/automation to audio, reducing CPU but changing the editable project structure depending on destination options.
myth: bounce track in place has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Save a Project Alternative, bounce one duplicated software-instrument track to a new track, mute the source, and compare.

correction: Region in Place commits selected region-level and channel processing according to its dialog choices; it is more local than bouncing the complete track.
myth: bounce region in place has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region or project, bounce one region to a new track, and compare boundaries, tails, and processing.

correction: Bounce-and-replace all tracks is a large project-structure change intended for consolidation; it should not be used casually as a CPU troubleshooting first step.
myth: bounce and replace all tracks has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Create a complete Project Alternative or project copy, run the operation only on a test copy, and verify every resulting track and routing relationship.

correction: Track export creates one file per selected track and has separate choices for effects, automation, tails, range, naming, and multi-output instruments.
myth: export selected tracks as audio files has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Export two representative tracks with the intended recipient settings and verify alignment, length, channel format, and processing before exporting the complete set.

correction: Export All Tracks produces separate track files, while true stems may be intentional submixes such as drums, vocals, or guitars; clarify the recipient’s definition before exporting.
myth: export all tracks and stem delivery has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Export a small test set from the same start point, then import it into a blank project to verify alignment and summed result.

correction: A multi-output instrument can be exported per track or per channel strip; those choices produce different file sets and must match the intended downstream workflow.
myth: exporting multi-output software instruments has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Export one multi-output instrument both ways in a test folder and inspect which outputs, auxes, and naming relationships are created.

correction: Effects, volume/pan automation, sends, and output processing can be included or excluded at different stages; the recipient’s goal determines which should be printed.
myth: including effects and automation in exports has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Export one representative track dry and processed from the same range, then document exactly what each file includes.

correction: A bounce difference can come from range, tails, realtime dependencies, random or free-running instruments, external hardware, missing inputs, Low Latency behavior, normalization, or monitoring—not one universal export bug.
myth: bounce sounds different from playback has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Bounce a short reproducible section realtime and offline with normalization off, then compare through the same playback path.

correction: Freeze renders a temporary audio file and deactivates the original processing for playback, reducing CPU while preserving a relatively easy path back to editing.
myth: track freeze as reversible cpu relief has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Freeze one confirmed CPU-heavy track in a Project Alternative, play the heaviest section, and compare CPU/drive meters and sound.

correction: Source Only freezes the instrument/source before track effects, while Pre Fader includes track effect plug-ins; the intended editability and CPU bottleneck determine the mode.
myth: freeze source only versus pre fader has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Freeze a duplicated CPU-heavy instrument once in Source Only and once Pre Fader, then compare CPU use and what remains editable.

correction: A frozen track plays its freeze file and blocks content edits until it is unfrozen; unfreezing restores the original regions, instrument, and plug-ins.
myth: unfreezing and returning to editability has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Freeze and then unfreeze a duplicated test track before relying on the workflow, confirming that the original edit state returns.

correction: Freeze prioritizes reversible CPU relief, while Bounce in Place creates a normal audio track/file and is better when the user intentionally wants to commit or edit audio.
myth: freeze versus bounce in place has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: On a duplicate instrument track, test Freeze and Track in Place separately, then compare recovery, CPU use, and downstream editing.

correction: System Overload can reflect processing-thread saturation, disk I/O, memory pressure, or one selected software-instrument live thread; the Performance Meter helps identify the bottleneck.
myth: diagnosing system overload: cpu versus disk has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Open the Performance Meter, replay the exact failing section, and note whether processing threads or drive I/O peaks first before changing anything.

correction: A larger I/O buffer usually provides more processing headroom but increases monitoring latency; the useful setting depends on whether the current task is recording or mixing.
myth: i/o buffer size and playback cpu headroom has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Save the current setting, raise the buffer one step for the failing mix passage, and compare overload behavior without recording.

correction: Software instruments can consume CPU through polyphony, oversampling, unison, sample streaming, and live-track processing; selecting a track may keep it on a live processing thread.
myth: software-instrument cpu and voice management has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Identify one instrument that peaks the Performance Meter, reduce one expensive voice/quality setting or freeze it, and replay the same passage.

correction: CPU cost and plug-in latency are different properties; bypass tests, Performance Meter changes, and plug-in latency help tags answer different questions.
myth: identifying expensive plug-ins has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: On a Project Alternative, bypass one suspected plug-in at a time during the failing section and log CPU and latency changes.

correction: Logic can leave unneeded tracks inactive and load their plug-ins when the track becomes relevant; selecting or monitoring a track may activate its processing.
myth: dynamic plug-in loading and inactive tracks has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Observe a dimmed inactive track, select it, and watch whether plug-in loading or CPU use changes before reorganizing the project.

correction: Optimization should target the measured bottleneck while preserving recoverability: buffer, freeze, voice count, sample storage, unused tracks, and project alternatives solve different problems.
myth: project optimization without destroying editability has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Create a Project Alternative, identify the actual bottleneck, apply one optimization, and rerun the exact problem section.

correction: Plug-in delay compensation keeps playback paths synchronized by delaying lower-latency paths to match the highest relevant latency; it does not remove the performer’s monitoring delay.
myth: plug-in delay compensation concept has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Create a Project Alternative, toggle the documented compensation mode for a short playback-only test, and compare timing without recording.

correction: Off, Audio and Software Instrument Tracks, and All cover different parts of Logic’s signal graph; aux and output plug-ins require broader compensation.
myth: pdc compensation modes has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: In a Project Alternative with a known latency plug-in on an aux/output, compare the narrower and All modes during playback.

correction: Latency on auxes and the Stereo Out can affect many tracks and may require the All compensation mode; the monitoring path can still feel delayed while recording.
myth: aux and output plug-in latency has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Temporarily bypass one high-latency aux/output processor in a Project Alternative and compare track alignment and live monitoring separately.

correction: Logic’s latency compensation also affects automation and sidechain timing, so timing problems can involve the detector path or automated control rather than only audible tracks.
myth: pdc with automation and sidechains has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the project state, use a simple transient trigger and automation marker, then bypass the suspected latency plug-in to test alignment.

correction: Logic can display a plug-in’s reported latency in samples/time, but that number is not the same as CPU usage or complete round-trip latency.
myth: reading a plug-in’s reported latency has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Hover over suspected plug-in slots, record their reported latency, then bypass one at a time and compare monitoring.

correction: Low Latency Mode bypasses latency-inducing plug-ins and disables sends on record-enabled, input-monitored, or focused instrument paths when the total exceeds the configured limit.
myth: low latency mode behavior has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Save the current project state, turn on Low Latency Mode, and inspect which plug-ins and sends change color/state before recording a test pass.

correction: A send can be marked Low Latency Safe so a necessary cue effect remains active, but the return path still must not exceed an acceptable monitoring delay.
myth: low latency safe sends has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Mark only the required monitoring reverb send Low Latency Safe and compare cue latency and sound against the disabled state.

correction: Lookahead limiters, linear-phase processors, oversampling, and other mastering plug-ins can add monitoring latency even when playback remains compensated.
myth: mastering chains during recording has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Create a tracking Project Alternative, bypass the output mastering chain, enable Low Latency Mode, and compare the same live cue.

correction: Lookahead, linear-phase filtering, and some oversampling modes require buffering that can increase plug-in latency; the exact amount is processor-specific.
myth: lookahead, linear phase, and oversampling latency has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: On a duplicate project state, switch one suspected processor to its lower-latency or realtime-quality mode and compare its reported latency and sound.

correction: Bypassing or removing a latency-reporting plug-in can change the compensation graph; compare after Logic has updated rather than nudging regions immediately.
myth: timing changes after bypassing a latency plug-in has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the project, bypass one latency plug-in, restart playback from before the test point, and compare timing after the engine updates.

correction: Playback pre-roll lets Logic begin processing before the visible start so transients at the start position are not missed when high compensation is active.
myth: playback pre-roll with high pdc has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Enable the documented playback pre-roll setting in a Project Alternative and compare a transient starting exactly at the playhead.

correction: PDC aligns processed playback paths; Recording Delay offsets captured-region placement; I/O buffer and hardware determine much of the live cue delay. These solve different problems.
myth: pdc versus recording delay and monitoring latency has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Record a repeatable loopback or transient test in a Project Alternative, separately measure monitoring feel and recorded placement, then change only the relevant setting.

correction: A track is the arrangement object that holds regions and points to a channel strip; the channel strip owns the instrument, inserts, sends, pan, fader, and routing.
myth: track versus channel strip has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Create a new empty track with the same channel strip in a Project Alternative, then change one shared channel-strip parameter and observe both tracks.

correction: A region is a time-bounded piece of audio/MIDI content placed on a track; track-level processing and controls normally affect every region routed through that track.
myth: region versus track has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate one region to a new independent track and compare a region edit with a track plug-in change.

correction: An audio region is a nondestructive reference to all or part of an audio file; many region edits change playback without rewriting the source file.
myth: audio region versus underlying audio file has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate an audio region, trim the duplicate nondestructively, and confirm the full source remains in the Project Audio Browser.

correction: A MIDI region stores note/controller events; the software-instrument plug-in lives on the channel strip, so changing the instrument normally affects every MIDI region using that strip.
myth: midi region versus software instrument has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region to a new track with duplicate settings, choose a different instrument there, and compare against changing the original shared channel strip.

correction: Duplicating a track creates an empty track with duplicated instrument/effect settings, while copying regions separately determines what musical content appears on it.
myth: duplicate track settings versus copying content has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate a track, leave it empty, then Option-drag one region and verify that processing is independent from the original channel strip.

correction: Logic can create multiple tracks that point to one channel strip, allowing separate region lanes but shared instrument, plug-ins, routing, fader, and automation ownership.
myth: multiple tracks using one channel strip has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Create a second track with the same channel strip in a Project Alternative and test mute/region organization versus a shared plug-in change.

correction: A copied region is normally an independent region object, but audio copies may still reference the same underlying audio file and MIDI aliases are a separate linked concept.
myth: copied regions and independence has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Copy one region, edit a region parameter or MIDI note in the copy, and verify whether the original changes.

correction: A MIDI alias references a parent region, so event edits to the parent propagate to aliases; converting an alias to a region copy breaks that linkage.
myth: midi aliases versus independent copies has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Create one alias and one ordinary copy from a duplicate MIDI region, edit the parent note, and compare both.

correction: Audio regions can be copied, looped, or repeated as clones, but all may still derive from the same source file; object linkage and file identity are separate questions.
myth: audio region copies, clones, and loops has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Create a normal copy and a repeated clone/loop in a test track, change a safe region parameter, and inspect source-file references.

correction: Region parameters such as transpose, delay, gain, quantize, loop, and Flex & Follow affect selected regions, while Track inspector and channel-strip parameters affect the track path.
myth: region parameters versus track parameters has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Duplicate the region, change one obvious region parameter, then compare it with a track/channel-strip change.

correction: Deleting a region removes the arrangement reference; the audio file may remain in the Project Audio Browser or project folder. Deleting the file itself is a separate and potentially destructive action.
myth: deleting a region versus deleting the recording file has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: In a project copy, delete one region from the Tracks area, verify the file remains in Project Audio, then undo.

correction: Tracks-area and region edits are often nondestructive references, while Audio File Editor operations, file deletion, and Optimize File can alter or remove source data.
myth: destructive versus nondestructive editing in logic has one universally correct setting, scope, or workflow.
safer_principle: Preserve a baseline, establish the correct owner and scope, then use one bounded test: Copy the project and source file, perform one region-level edit, and compare it with the clearly labeled file-level operation without saving the destructive test.

correction: Controller data may carry sustain, expression, articulation, pitch, and intentional performance gestures; identify the event type and scope first.
myth: All non-note MIDI data is accidental and can be safely deleted.
safer_principle: Identify the exact Logic object or signal stage, preserve a baseline, and run one reversible test.

correction: They act at different layers and may be mapped differently by the instrument.
